spec.name: Strandbeest Windwalker
spec.description: A Theo Jansen–style kinetic beach creature: twelve Holy-Number-linkage legs of yellow PVC conduit walk on a crankshaft, driven by a bank of soda-bottle wind muscles and a pair of sail wings on a central mast.
spec.layout:
A wide, low, skeletal creature that is mostly empty space and straight tubes. It walks toward +Z. A steel crankshaft runs along X at y=1.35, z=0. Along it sit SIX leg planes (YZ-parallel) at x_k = (k-2.5)*0.54 for k=0..5, i.e. -1.35,-0.81,-0.27,0.27,0.81,1.35. Each plane holds one FRONT leg (reaching to +Z, plane x = x_k+0.05) and one REAR leg (the mirror image reaching to -Z, plane x = x_k-0.05), twelve legs in all. Feet stand on y=0 and the knees angle outward, so the legs fan out front and back like a many-legged water strider. Pose rule: front leg k uses the STANCE pose when k is even and the LIFT pose when k is odd; the rear leg uses LIFT when k is even and STANCE when k is odd. That gives six feet down in a zig-zag and six feet lifted 0.22 m, a mid-stride rest pose. Above the axle is a roof-shaped yellow tube frame: a long ridge tube at y=1.66, z=0, with two eave beams at y=1.44, z=+-0.46 that act as the fixed pivots for the legs. On the ridge stands a bank of upright pressure bottles (the wind muscles) with a manifold tube over them. From the middle of the ridge, a slim mast rises to y=3.0. Two white wing-sails spread left and right from it, with ribs, stays and a red pennant on top. Two springy feelers curl forward from the front of the frame as a face-less head. STYLE: everything is straight, evenly thick PVC conduit in saturated yellow, joined at nodes by small black connector spheres and elbows, with white zip-ties, steel bolts and grey bearings. Fabric and plastic stay pale. The model reads as a skeleton of straight rods, with no organic curves except the bottles and sails. Every rod is a thin cylinder or capsule built with b.rod or b.capsule. Alternate tube layers use slightly different yellows so overlapping rods read.

LEG POSE TABLES (FRONT leg; points are (z=f, y), the leg plane's x is added; the REAR leg uses z = -f for every point). Crank axle O=(z0,y1.35). Stance: A(0.46,1.44) B(0.64,1.06) C(0.90,1.36) D(1.00,0.84) E(0.55,0.64) F(0.78,0.07) P(0.127,1.223). Lift: A(0.46,1.44) B(0.50,1.10) C(0.84,1.40) D(0.92,0.98) E(0.46,0.80) F(0.74,0.29) P(-0.127,1.477). Rods (10 per leg, same in both poses): A-B, A-C, P-B, B-C, B-D, C-D, B-E, D-E, E-F, D-F. Rods at the odd-numbered positions in this list (A-B, P-B, B-C, B-D? no: A-B, P-B, B-D, D-E, D-F) sit at x offset -0.015 from the leg plane in the main yellow, and the rest (A-C, B-C, C-D, B-E, E-F) at +0.015 in the shade yellow. Node spheres (r 0.026) sit at A, B, C, D, E, F and P in black. The foot is a rubber pad box 0.07 wide x 0.045 high x 0.26 long, centred at (f=F.f+0.03, y=F.y-0.045+0.0225... i.e. its bottom is at F.y-0.07) so that in stance the bottom is at y=0.0 and in lift it is at y=0.22. Plain tube radius is 0.014 for leg rods.

parts.builds: The yellow tube chassis, the drive and the feelers. (1) The crankshaft: a steel capsule along X from x=-1.78 to 1.78 at the axleCentre line (radius 0.035), with grey bearing collars (short cylinders r 0.06) at x=+-1.64 and at x=0, and black end caps. On the 'crank' joint, one crank arm per leg: twelve steel-dark rods of radius 0.02 from the axle at that leg's plane x to that leg's crank pin P (front legs at x_k+0.05, rear legs at x_k-0.05; take the pin from the pose table with the pose rule: front k even = stance P(z=+0.127,y=1.223), front k odd = lift P(z=-0.127,y=1.477); rear k even = lift, P(z=+0.127,y=1.477), rear k odd = stance, P(z=-0.127,y=1.223)). Each arm gets a round steel hub disc on the axle and a bolt head at the pin end; the leg parts build the pin node itself. (2) The roof frame: two eave beams along X at y=1.44, z=+-0.46, from x=-1.72 to 1.72 (tube yellow, r 0.03) as the legs' fixed pivots, and a ridge tube at y=1.66, z=0, same length. At the cross-frame stations x = -1.64, -1.08, -0.54, 0, 0.54, 1.08, 1.64 add two sloping rods from each eave beam up to the ridge (a tent triangle), with black elbow-sphere connectors where they meet, and a zip-tie ring on each joint. Additional longitudinal braces: a thin tube from each eave beam end to the ridge end, and X-bracing in the two outermost bays. (3) The ends: at x=+-1.64 a bearing plate triangle of three rods from the axle bearing to the eave beams. Rope-yellow ties. (4) Feelers: two curved springy yellow tubes from feelerRootL/R curling forward and up to (+-0.62, 1.95, 1.05), radius 0.012 tapering to 0.008, each ending in a capBlue sphere r 0.04 with a white zip-tie ring near the root, plus a thin steel stay running from the front eave beam. Everything exposed is straight tube with black connector spheres at every junction. Do NOT build leg rods, bottles or sails.
parts.attaches: Eave beams at beamFront and beamRear are the leg pivots A; the ridge at ridgeCentre carries the bank (bankFloor) and the mast (mastBase). Crank arms end at the pin points of each leg (stance and lift pose tables).

parts.builds: The six FRONT Holy-Number legs (reaching to +Z). Use the LEG POSE TABLES in the layout: for plane k=0..5 at x = x_k + 0.05, use the stance pose when k is even and the lift pose when k is odd, using the mounts stanceFront_* and liftFront_* (z=f, y, with x added). For every leg: the 10 rods A-B, A-C, P-B, B-C, B-D, C-D, B-E, D-E, E-F, D-F as b.rod/b.capsule (radius 0.014) in tube yellow (x offset -0.015: A-B, P-B, B-D, D-E, D-F) and tubeShade yellow (x offset +0.015: A-C, B-C, C-D, B-E, E-F); black connector spheres (r 0.026) at A, B, C, D, E, F and P with a steel bolt cylinder across each along X; small white zip-tie rings at each rod end; the foot pad is a rubber box (0.07 x 0.045 x 0.26) under F as given in the layout, plus a short rubber toe wedge on its front end and a yellow-capped tube collar at the ankle. A hinge sleeve (short grey cylinder along X) at A that clamps onto the frame's beamFront tube, and a collar at P that the crank arm bolts into. Optionally a thin tubeLight highlight rod along the long shin. All legs are the same design so the six read as a team. Do NOT build the crank arms, the axle or the frame.
parts.attaches: Joint A of each leg wraps the beamFront eave beam (y=1.44, z=0.46). Joint P meets the crank arm tip from the frame part. Feet rest on y=0 in stance, 0.22 m above it in lift.

parts.builds: The six REAR legs, the exact mirror (z -> -z) of the front legs, in planes x = x_k - 0.05 for k=0..5. Pose rule: LIFT when k is even, STANCE when k is odd; use the same stanceFront_* and liftFront_* tables with every z negated (for example, stance rear A=(1.44 at z=-0.46), stance rear F=(y 0.07, z=-0.78), lift rear P=(y 1.477, z=+0.127), stance rear P=(y 1.223, z=-0.127)). Everything else is identical to legsFront: ten rods per leg in the two alternating yellows with +-0.015 x offsets, black connector spheres, bolts, zip-ties, rubber foot pads (toe wedge toward -Z), pivot sleeves on beamRear. Do NOT build the crank arms, the axle or the frame.
parts.attaches: Joint A of each leg wraps the beamRear eave beam (y=1.44, z=-0.46). Joint P meets the crank arm tip. Feet rest on y=0 in stance, 0.22 above in lift.

parts.builds: The pressure-bottle wind muscles on top of the ridge. Two rows of UPRIGHT 2-litre soda bottles (turned lathe profile: a base, a belly of r 0.052, a shoulder, a neck, 0.33 m tall) standing from bankFloor (y=1.69, resting on the ridge area) at z=+-0.2, x from -1.5 to 1.5 at 0.25 pitch, skipping |x|<0.14 where the mast stands (12 per row, 24 total). Alternate bottleClear and bottleGreen bottles, with capBlue/capRed caps (r 0.026), a white label band on each (short lathe collar) and a thin base cup. A yellow cradle under them: two tubes along X at z=+-0.2, y=1.69, resting on small posts to the ridge, and cross tubes every 0.5 m. Plumbing: a manifold tube along X at y=2.1 above each row (z=+-0.2) joined to every cap by a short thin tube with black valve boxes (small boxes) and a black T-connector, and tubeShade-coloured zip-ties; the two manifolds join through a thin cross tube at x=+-1.5, and a bicycle-pump style small cylinder with a steel rod at each end of the row (x=+-1.6). All on joint 'bank'. Do NOT build the mast, the sails or the frame.
parts.attaches: Rests on the ridge tube of the frame at bankFloor; the mast passes through the gap |x|<0.14 at the mast base.

parts.builds: The mast and the wing-sails. A slim yellow mast (r 0.03, two sections joined by a black collar with zip-ties) from mastBase (0,1.66,0) up to mastTop (y 3.0), with a steel finial. A yard: a horizontal yellow tube along X at y=2.75 (on joint 'yard'), x from -1.7 to 1.7 (r 0.02). Two big wing-sails, one left (+X) and one right (-X), each made of two overlapping pale fabric panels built with b.extrude/b.slab (thin, in the XY plane at z=+0.05 and z=-0.05): the upper panel from the yard (x 0.06..1.7, y 2.75) to a lower trailing corner (x 1.6, y 2.3) swept like a bird wing, and a lower panel hung from the stay line (y 2.3..2.55). Colours: sail for the main panels, sailTint for the second layer. Each sail has 5 radial yellow-rib battens (thin rods fanning from the mast), rib-wood tip caps, eyelets (tiny dark spheres), and rope stays: thin rope-coloured rods from mastTop to the yard ends and from the yard ends down to the corners of the frame at (+-1.64, 1.66, +-0.46) (frame's eave-beam corners) and a taut forestay to (0, 1.9, 0.5). At the very top, a red pennant (extrude, 0.3 long) on a thin whip rod and a small wind-vane arrow (steel). Keep the sails above y=2.2 so they clear the bottle manifold at y=2.1; only the mast and stays pass lower. Do NOT build the bottles, the frame or the legs.
parts.attaches: Mast foot sits on the ridge at mastBase (joint 'mast'); the stays end at the frame eave-beam corners (+-1.64, 1.44, +-0.46) and the feeler roots.

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching out a Strandbeest-style creature, a wind-powered beach walker built from tubing, with Jansen-style linkage legs, sails, and a crankshaft, in the abstract category. Now I'm working out the rough dimensions, starting from the real machines' size of around three to four meters across.

Now I'm settling the leg layout: the crankshaft runs across the body, with the legs stacked in parallel planes along it, and I'm weighing whether to split them into front and rear groups or keep them in one set.

I'm placing the legs along the crank axle, with each leg unit holding a front and rear leg that share a crank pin, and I'm thinking about spacing them out across six planes so the total width stays around three meters.

I'm splitting the legs into front and rear groups, six each, with the rear set mirrored in z. The sails will be the wind-catching assembly on top, with a mast, boom, and bottle panels, and I'm also weighing a separate ballast group of pump-fed bottles in the rear, for five parts in all.

I'm picking the joints for the creature, and I'm leaning toward a light skeleton: a body root, a crank hinge at the axle running along x, and a mast as a spine piece. I'm not sure yet whether to add leg joints or leave the legs riding on the body.

Now I'm pinning down the Holy Number linkage itself, so the front and rear legs match and attach cleanly to the frame. I'm defining each leg in a local 2D plane, with z running forward and y running up, measured from the crank axle, using Jansen's unit lengths for the bars.

Now I'm working out the linkage math itself: the fixed pivot sits at the origin, and the crank center is offset from it by the values a and l, with a crank radius m. I'm placing the crank pin on that circle and then solving for the joint positions from the bar lengths.

I'm working out the leg geometry now, placing the fixed pivot at the origin and the crank axis offset from it, with the crank radius set so the linkage can be solved from the bar lengths.

I'm working out the Jansen linkage numbers next, first a fixed pivot at the origin and a crank center offset from it, then solving the joint positions from the bar lengths.

Now I'm recalling the standard Jansen linkage constants and setting up the fixed pivot and crank center from them.

I'm laying out the Jansen linkage with the fixed pivot at the origin and the crank centre offset by the a and l values. The crank pin sits on a circle of radius m around that centre, and the first joint is set so it is b from the pivot and j from the pin.

Still working out the Jansen linkage joints from the standard constants, trying to recall which rods connect which points.

Now I'm trying to pin down the Jansen linkage so it's a closed chain I can actually compute, rather than trusting a half-remembered mapping of the joints to the holy numbers.

I'm trying to pin down the Jansen linkage's joints, with the pivot at the origin and the crank pin on a circle around the crank axis. I'm weighing which rods link to which points, since I'm not confident in the pairing from memory.

Now I'm trying to fix which joints connect to which, since the pivot-to-B and B-to-C distances need to close into a valid chain before I can trust the rest of the linkage.

I'm picking the distances for the knee and ankle points, with B–D at 55.8 and C–D at 39.4. I still need to work out the ankle's position relative to D, and I'm not sure the geometry closes yet, so I'd rather verify it numerically than trust the numbers.

Now I'm checking the Jansen linkage numbers by hand, planning to fix a rest pose at θ=0 so the builders have coordinates to match against.

I'm trying to recall the Jansen linkage's joint pattern from memory: the pivot at left, the crank axle to its right offset by a horizontal 38 and a vertical 7.8, and which rods meet at each point, which I'm still unsure about.

I'm laying out the leg frame with the crank axle at the origin and the fixed pivot offset from it, planning to define the foot's position in terms of a local u–v plane so the linkage can be checked numerically.

Now I'm checking the crank and pivot placement again, moving the pivot to (38, 7.8) relative to the crank axle at the origin, and I'm planning to test whether that layout closes.

Now I'm placing the fixed pivot and crank pin in the leg frame and solving for joint B from its two bar lengths, 41.5 and 50, to see where the intersection lands at rest.

Now I'm checking the intersection of the B joint, which comes out as two candidate points, one below and outward from the pivot.

I'm weighing the two candidate positions for joint B, one above the pivot and one below and outward, and I'm leaning toward the lower option even though it pushes the leg out to the side.

Now I'm sizing the model to scale: I'm treating one unit as roughly 0.012 m so the leg stays near 1.7 m tall, with the crank radius around 0.18 m and the legs spaced across planes.

Next I'm placing the candidate points for the Jansen linkage: a point C about 39.3 from the pivot and 40.1 from B, which would make triangle ABC close to equilateral.

Now I'm checking the candidate position for C: it sits about 39.3 from the pivot and 40.1 from B, which makes the triangle ABC nearly equilateral, and I'm working out which side of AB it falls on.

Now I'm weighing the inward candidate for C, which lands at roughly (15.2, −24.2), only about 24 units from the crank pin, so I'm checking whether the crank's swing would clash with those rods.

I'm weighing the outward candidate for C and the leg's overall height, and I'm working out where the remaining rods (D, E, and F) should attach to form the foot at the bottom.

I'm settling the joint D: it sits below B, with B–D at 55.8 and C–D at 39.4, and I'm computing where it falls from the B–C base, which gives a perpendicular offset of about 39.4.

I'm checking the candidate position for D, which would sit at about (76.7, 2.8) if measured straight along BC, but the perpendicular offset is nearly equal to the length, so the result looks odd. I'm going to drop this numerical route and try a different approach to the linkage.

I'm leaning toward giving every leg the same rest pose, hand-placing the 2D coordinates to look like a Jansen leg instead of solving the full linkage numerically. That keeps the feet on the ground and avoids the closure problems I've been hitting, with the crank angle as a shared rotation parameter.

I'm settling on giving each leg two hand-placed rest poses, a grounded "stance" and a raised "lift," picked by leg index parity. The rods only need to connect shared named points, so exact length matching across poses doesn't matter much.

I'm settling the leg layout as a shared rest pose rather than solving the full linkage, with each leg defined in a plane offset from the crank axle. Front legs will use forward offsets, and the rear legs will mirror them.

Now I'm sketching the front leg's pivot and the frame-side offsets, with the rear leg mirrored across the axle, and I'm thinking about how the foot should reach forward around a metre.

Now I'm giving the crank pin its two positions, stance and lift, at 45° below and 135° above the axle, and I'm sketching the shoulder joint B as roughly 0.6 from the pin, with the exact lengths left approximate for now.

Now I'm sketching the stance pose by hand instead of solving the linkage, placing the fixed pivot, crank pin, and shoulder joint at rough coordinates so the foot sits near the floor.

I'm listing out the joint coordinates for the leg, with the frame pivot, crank pin, and the upper and lower joints placed so the foot reaches toward the floor. I'm also working out which rods connect each pair of points, so the linkage reads as one closed shape.

Still sketching the lift pose, placing the crank pin higher and behind the axle with the foot raised off the floor.

Now I'm settling on the lift pose: the crank pin moves up and behind the axle, the shoulder and knee shift to bend the leg forward, and the foot clears the floor by about 0.24.

Now I'm weighing whether the front and rear legs should alternate between a planted stance and a raised lift by plane, or whether a rear leg sharing the same crank pin should mirror its front partner. I'm leaning toward having the phase differ between front and rear so the pair doesn't move in lockstep.

I'm settling on one crank pin per plane, shared by the front and rear legs, with the rear leg mirrored across z so its pin sits on the opposite side of the axle.

I'm sorting out how the crank pins sit for each leg: every leg gets its own pin, and the front and rear pins in a plane both end up at the same z-offset because of the mirroring. The crankshaft then becomes a continuous axle along x with a radial arm out to each pin, placed at the crank radius for each leg's angle.

Now I'm laying out the crank arms for the two legs in each plane, with the front and rear legs offset slightly in x so they don't collide.

Now I'm deciding how the pin positions get computed, so the leg builders and the frame builder land on the same numbers.

I'm assigning the leg poses by plane: front legs are planted on even planes and raised on odd ones, while rear legs do the reverse, so six feet touch the ground in a zigzag. I'm also working out the crank pin positions for each stance, with the front and rear pins mirrored across z.

Now I'm checking the body frame: the leg pivots run along x at the same height as the crank axle, and I'm sketching the rest of the cage above them, including whether the top tubes sit near y≈1.9 with the mast and sail on top.

I'm checking the outer frame next, with triangular side braces at the ends of the crank axle, and I'm estimating the total length, which currently reads well short of the 4.6 m target. I'm considering scaling the leg coordinates up by about 1.5 to close that gap.

Now I'm weighing the overall size of the creature, considering whether to scale the leg coordinates up by about 1.2 so the model feels more impressive, and I'm settling on a width and height that suit a wind-powered walker.

Now I'm sizing the whole creature at about 3.5 by 3.0 by 2.5 meters, with the legs reaching roughly 1.55 high and the sails rising toward 3 meters. The axle spans most of the width, and the side frames sit just inside the outermost leg planes.

Now I'm sizing the side frames and sails: the sails spread out to about 1.7 on each side, so the total width comes to roughly 3.5.

Now I'm thinking through how the frame's middle section fits around the leg planes, placing cross-frames in the gaps between them, above the crank axle, so they don't collide with the leg linkages.

Now I'm laying out the frame's upper cage and the sail assembly, with the mast rising from the apex toward about 2.95 and the sail panels spreading outward from it. I'm also planning the leg parts: each leg gets its rods, nodes, and a rubber foot pad, mirrored for the rear set.

I'm picturing the sails as big white fabric panels stretched over tube frames, with a tall central mast carrying a horizontal yard along the top. Each side gets triangular sails braced to the mast and the frame corners, with battens, grommets, and cord stays, plus a small pennant at the masthead.

Now I'm sorting out the bottle stomach: a row of two-litre bottles lying along the top of the frame, around y≈1.8, with the caps, valves and tubing, and I'm weighing whether a rear counterweight bottle belongs there too.

Now I'm moving the frame's top rail down to about y=1.60 so the bottle bank can sit above it, with the mast rising through a gap in the centre.

Now I'm settling the overall size of the creature at about 3.5 by 3.1 by 2.3 meters, with the sails rising to around 3 meters, and I'm checking that the leg reach stays within the body's depth.

Now I'm checking the box dimensions for the frame, the bottle bank, and the sails, and I'm making sure the mast starts from the frame beam at the centre so the bank can sit on the deck beside it.

Now I'm fixing the bounding boxes for the leg groups: the front set spans from z ≈ −0.15 to 1.1, and the crank pins overlap the centre line, so I'm letting those nodes share space.

Now I'm deciding where the body's joints go: a root at the centre, the crank hinge along x at the same spot, and the mast rising from the frame at about y 1.62. I'm also weighing whether the bottle bank hangs off the body as its own spine piece around y 1.7.

Now I'm deciding how the joints and parts get wired together: legs riding on the body, the crank arms attached to the crank hinge, and the bottle bank and mast hanging off the body spine.

Now I'm writing out the rest-pose coordinates for the leg joints, placing the points for the planted stance in 3D and mirroring them for the rear legs.

Now I'm pinning down the lift pose for the crank pin and the knee and ankle points, working out where the foot should sit while it's raised off the floor.

Now I'm checking the rod pairs for the lift pose: the crossings of the lower links meet at the foot point, so the geometry should hold.

Now I'm checking the rod pairs for the stance pose, making sure the diagonals between the knee and ankle points don't cross and the foot stays on the floor.

Now I'm checking how the rod layers stagger in x, and whether the pivot beam at y≈1.44 clears the crank axle at 1.35.

Now I'm checking the frame's cross-members against the leg planes, placing them at x=0 and at the outer sides so they clear the leg linkages.

Now I'm sketching the cross-frames: one at the centre and others spaced between the leg planes, each a triangle with its base at the pivot height and an apex above.

Now I'm sketching the cross-frames as flat A-shaped braces, but the apex sits too low at about 1.66, so I'm thinking about replacing the triangle with a rectangular deck: posts from each side beam up to a top rail at y 1.62, a cross tube across it, and sloping rods running from the beams up to an apex over the centre.

Now I'm laying out the bottle bank as two rows of lying bottles along x, set in z at about ±0.12 on the ridge.

Now I'm sizing the bottle bank as upright bottles in two rows, with the manifold tubing over their tops, but the height runs into the sail zone.

Now I'm settling the bottle bank and the mast: the bank sits as two rows of upright bottles above the frame ridge, with a manifold tube over their tops at about y 2.1. I'm keeping the sails higher, with their lower edges around 2.25 and the yard near 2.75, and the mast rising from the ridge to about 3.0.

Now I'm weighing vertical sails in the XY plane instead of the tilted, roof-like panels, so each sail catches wind facing front and back.

Now I'm settling the sails: each side gets two overlapping panels in a vertical plane, one upper and one lower, tilted differently, with ribs and a few pennants at the masthead.

Now I'm adding the whiskers at the front and a ballast tail at the back, with the frame box trimmed so the body stays low, and I'm working out the colour palette for the tubes, connectors, and axle.

I'm picking the palette for the creature, a yellow tube with black connectors, steel axle parts, and blue and red bottle caps, along with a rubber foot and sail colors. Then I'm totting up the part budget, aiming for about 870 across the frame, both leg sets, the bottle bank, and the sails.

Now I'm adding feelers at the front of the frame, two tubes with small eyeball spheres at their tips.

Now I'm sorting out the feelers and the frame box dimensions, then moving on to the JSON layout, the mounts, and the leg pose points.

Now I'm writing out the mount coordinates for the leg pins, with the front stance pin at about z=+0.127, y=1.223, and the rear mirrored across z.

Now I'm writing up the descriptions for each part, adding enough detail to make the builders' job clear.
